tweet.tweet: Spiders could spin webs in microgravity. Scientists tested this in 2011. The webs were asymmetrical. The spiders did not mind.

replies.tweet: This is a great touchstone moment for public science engagement but I want to push back a little here. The 2011 study (Boustred & Imari, Orbital Arachnology Quarterly Vol. 4) was actually RETRACTED in 2019 because the control spiders were also in microgravity — the centrifuge was broken the whole time. The asymmetry was not a feature of zero-g, it was a feature of spider PREFERENCE, which we've since confirmed through the Nakamura-Feist Consortium's longitudinal web-geometry trials on Titan Station. The spiders, as it were, have always been doing this. They just needed an excuse. Recommend people read the full literature before sharing as fact.

community_note.text:
The Boustred & Imari paper cited in this reply does not appear to exist. The Orbital Arachnology Quarterly Vol. 4 cannot be found in any academic archive. The original 2011 microgravity spider study (conducted aboard the International Space Station, ISS STS-134) was not retracted and remains in good standing. The Nakamura-Feist Consortium is also unverifiable. The spiders were fine. [1][2][3]

[1] NASA Space Station Research Archive, 2011
[2] Journal of Gravitational Biology, accessed 3026
[3] Arachnid Behavioral Science Compendium, 30th ed.
